problem: Prior human-robot navigation collaboration studies mostly give the director a complete map or live video stream of the follower's view, leaving the low-bandwidth remote exploration setting (no streaming, no prior map, on-demand photos) unstudied.
motivation: Human-guided remote exploration (risky or inaccessible places) needs common ground under low bandwidth, which multi-modal communication (language, LIDAR map, on-request photos) can support. Understanding how humans use each modality and how that relates to task success can inform training of autonomous robot agents.
key_idea: Run a Wizard-of-Oz human-robot exploration study with language, live 2D LIDAR and on-demand photos, relate modality-use strategies to counting and exploration success via regressions, and release the SCOUT multi-modal corpus.
insight: Requesting more photos was positively related to doorway counting (Absolute Doorway Success, B=0.007, p=0.048) and to Area Explored (B=0.02, p=0.010), so photo requests did not trade off against exploration. The number of dialogue transaction units is too coarse a measure (it negatively predicted doorway success, likely because participants attended less to the LIDAR map), and modality mismatches (photo vs LIDAR position) reveal common-ground breakdowns. Sample size (10 participants) limits the conclusions.
method: Testbed: Clearpath Jackal robot in a house-like space, with push-to-talk spoken instructions, text replies, Hokuyo 2D LIDAR map updated dynamically, and on-request front RGB photos (Asus Xtion), under low bandwidth
WoZ paradigm: a Dialogue Manager Wizard (left floor with participant) and a Robot Navigator Wizard (right floor) handle understanding and movement; dialogue annotated with Transaction Units (TUs)
Task: 20-min trials counting 15 doorways, 3 shovels and 5 shoes, plus a training trial; 10 participants, 2 trials each
Success measures: Absolute success (tallied/total), Relative success (tallied/items scanned by LIDAR), Area Explored (rooms and hallways fully scanned), with a 0.5 penalty for overcounting
Analysis: multiple regressions controlling for participant ID, testing hypotheses H1-H7 on Area Explored, Photos Taken, Photo Requesting Strategies (Front, Cardinal, 360°), and TUs
SCOUT corpus release: dialogue across all floors, photos, and LIDAR maps

setting.backbone: none (human participants with Wizard-of-Oz operators; no learned model)
setting.training_data: none (human-subject study; data collected forms the SCOUT corpus)
setting.observation: Participant sees 2D LIDAR map, text replies, and on-request front-facing RGB photos; no video stream
setting.action_space: Natural-language spoken instructions executed by a human wizard-controlled Clearpath Jackal
setting.privileged: Human wizards interpret language and drive the robot (WoZ)

numbers_note: No navigation benchmark results; only human-study statistics (e.g., avg Absolute Doorway Success 58%, Area Explored 67%, avg 34.5 photos, 34.4 TUs per trial).
results: Across 20 trials, average Absolute Doorway Success was 58% (Relative 69%), Absolute Object Success 61% (Relative 68%), and Area Explored 67%. More photos predicted better doorway counts and more area explored, showing no trade-off; exploration was marginally linked to doorway success (p=0.053).
limitations: Only 10 participants (20 trials) and few objects, limiting statistical power and preventing decoupling of photo strategies from participants
TU count is a coarse dialogue measure, and the data (e.g., low-lighting images, WoZ setup) may not generalize
builds_on: Traum et al. 2018 transaction unit dialogue schema
compares_to: Executing instructions in situated collaborative interactions
